Questions from previous NIOS papers show the exam they appeared in.

questions.q: The extent of ionisation of a weak acid and its strength are —

questions.q: The conjugate base of H2SO4 is —

The unit of K_sp for AgCl is —

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark.

questions.q: (a) Define Brønsted–Lowry acid. (b) Write the conjugate base of H2O.
questions.answer: (a) A substance that donates a proton (H+). (b) OH−.

questions.q: Identify the conjugate acid–base pairs in: NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH−.
questions.answer: NH3 (base) and NH4+ (its conjugate acid); H2O (acid) and OH− (its conjugate base).

questions.q: State true or false: (a) The pH of a neutral solution at 298 K is 7. (b) The solubility product of a salt changes with the concentration of the ions.
questions.answer: (a) True. (b) False – K_sp depends only on temperature.

questions.q: Write the K_sp expression for (a) AgCl (b) CaF2.
Fill in: (a) The pH of pure water at 298 K is ______. (b) pH + pOH = ______.
Match: (a) Strong acid (b) Weak base (c) Acidic buffer with (i) NH4OH (ii) HCl (iii) CH3COOH + CH3COONa.
Complete: (a) The salt of a weak acid and a strong base gives a ______ solution. (b) The common ion effect ______ the ionisation of a weak electrolyte.
Write (a) the relationship between K_a and K_b of a conjugate pair and (b) the Henderson equation for an acidic buffer.
questions.answer: (a) K_a × K_b = K_w. (b) pH = pK_a + log([salt]/[acid]).

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: What is a conjugate acid–base pair? Write the conjugate acid of a basic buffer's weak base NH3 and the conjugate base of HCl.
questions.answer: A pair of species that differ by one proton. The conjugate acid of NH3 is NH4+; the conjugate base of HCl is Cl−.

questions.q: What is a basic buffer? Give an example and explain how it works.
questions.answer: A solution of a weak base and its salt with a strong acid (NH4OH + NH4Cl). On adding acid, OH− of the base neutralises it; on adding base, NH4+ neutralises OH−, so the pH changes little.

questions.q: Why is H2SO3 called a diprotic acid? Which of K1 and K2 is larger?
questions.answer: It can donate two protons: H2SO3 ⇌ H+ + HSO3− (K1); HSO3− ⇌ H+ + SO3^2− (K2). K1 is larger because removing a proton from a negative ion is more difficult.

questions.q: Define the solubility product. Write its expression for Ag2CrO4.
questions.answer: The product of the molar concentrations of the ions of a sparingly soluble salt in a saturated solution, each raised to the power of its coefficient. K_sp = [Ag+]²[CrO4^2−].

questions.q: Why is an aqueous solution of NH4Cl acidic?
questions.answer: NH4+ ions hydrolyse: NH4+ + H2O ⇌ NH3 + H3O+, producing H3O+ ions, while Cl− does not react with water.

questions.q: State Ostwald's dilution law.
questions.answer: The degree of ionisation of a weak electrolyte increases on dilution; α = √(K_a/C), where C is the concentration.

questions.q: Calculate the pH of 0.001 M NaOH.
What is the common ion effect? Give an example.
questions.answer: Suppression of ionisation of a weak electrolyte by adding a strong electrolyte with a common ion; e.g. adding NH4Cl to NH4OH reduces [OH−].

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: The solubility of silver chloride is 1.3 × 10^-5 mol L^-1. Calculate its solubility product.
Write the two steps of ionisation of H2CO3 with K1 and K2. Which is larger and why? Compare the strengths of the two steps.
questions.answer: H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3− (K1 = 4.3 × 10^-7); HCO3− ⇌ H+ + CO3^2− (K2 = 4.7 × 10^-11). K1 > K2 because the second proton leaves a negatively charged ion, which holds H+ more strongly; so the first step is stronger as an acid.

questions.q: Calculate the pH of a buffer containing 0.1 M CH3COOH and 0.1 M CH3COONa (pK_a = 4.76). What is the pH after adding 0.01 M NaOH?
Explain hydrolysis of salts with examples of acidic, basic and neutral salts.
questions.answer: Hydrolysis is the reaction of the ions of a salt with water. NH4Cl (strong acid + weak base) gives an acidic solution; CH3COONa (weak acid + strong base) gives a basic solution; NaCl (strong acid + strong base) is neutral as neither ion hydrolyses.

questions.q: Calculate the pH of 0.1 M acetic acid (K_a = 1.8 × 10^-5).
Explain the Lewis concept of acids and bases with examples.
questions.answer: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair (BF3, AlCl3, H+); a Lewis base donates an electron pair (NH3, OH−, H2O). Their reaction forms a coordinate bond: BF3 + :NH3 → F3B←NH3.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: (a) State Ostwald's dilution law for a weak acid. (b) Calculate the degree of ionisation of 0.01 M CH3COOH (K_a = 1.8 × 10^-5). (c) Why does α increase on dilution?
questions.answer:
(a) For HA ⇌ H+ + A−, K_a = Cα²/(1 − α) ≈ Cα², so α = √(K_a/C).
(b) α = √(1.8 × 10^-5 / 0.01) = √(1.8 × 10^-3) = 0.0424 (4.24%).
(c) As C decreases, α = √(K_a/C) increases; ions meet less often, so more ionisation occurs.

questions.q: (a) What is a buffer solution? Name its types with an example. (b) Derive the Henderson equation. (c) Explain how an acidic buffer resists pH change.
questions.answer:
(a) A solution that resists change in pH on adding small amounts of acid or base; acidic buffer (CH3COOH + CH3COONa) and basic buffer (NH4OH + NH4Cl).
(b) K_a = [H+][A−]/[HA] → [H+] = K_a[HA]/[A−] → pH = pK_a + log([A−]/[HA]) = pK_a + log([salt]/[acid]).
(c) Added H+ reacts with CH3COO− to form CH3COOH; added OH− reacts with CH3COOH to form CH3COO− and water; the ratio salt/acid hardly changes.

questions.q: (a) Define the solubility product and its relation to solubility for AB, AB2 and A2B3 type salts. (b) The K_sp of Mg(OH)2 is 1.2 × 10^-11; find its solubility. (c) State the condition for precipitation.
questions.answer:
(a) K_sp = ionic product in a saturated solution; AB: K_sp = s²; AB2: K_sp = 4s³; A2B3: K_sp = 108s⁵.
(b) Mg(OH)2 ⇌ Mg^2+ + 2OH−; K_sp = s(2s)² = 4s³, so s³ = 1.2 × 10^-11/4 = 3 × 10^-12 and s = 1.44 × 10^-4 mol L^-1.
(c) A precipitate forms when the ionic product exceeds K_sp.

questions.q: Explain the Brønsted–Lowry theory with the conjugate pairs. Define amphoteric species and write the conjugate acid and base of HCO3−. Calculate pH of 0.05 M H2SO4 (assume complete ionisation).
questions.answer:
Acids donate protons and bases accept them; every acid HA gives a conjugate base A−, every base B a conjugate acid BH+; strong acids have weak conjugate bases.
Amphoteric species can act as both acid and base (H2O, HCO3−). Conjugate acid of HCO3− is H2CO3 and its conjugate base is CO3^2−.
[H+] = 2 × 0.05 = 0.1 M, pH = 1.
